content: Time should be allocated to reassuring respondents and addressing their questions. In addition to the BeSD survey questions mentioned earlier, countries may choose to include additional questions about the provision of COVID-19 vaccines. These questions, which are specifically designed for health workers, should only be included in data collection if they provide valuable descriptive data for the immunization program. For example, one question could assess health workers' willingness to recommend the COVID-19 vaccine to eligible individuals. The question might ask, Would you recommend a COVID-19 vaccine to eligible individuals? The percentage of health workers who respond yes would indicate their willingness to promote the vaccine. If COVID-19 vaccines are not yet available in a country, the question can be adapted to ask, Would you recommend a COVID-19 vaccine to eligible individuals when it becomes available? For instance, they might be asked, How confident are you that you could answer patient questions about getting a COVID-19 vaccine? Response options could range from Not at all confident to Very confident. This question evaluates health workers' ability to meet patients' informational needs regarding the vaccine. If the vaccine is not yet available, the question can be modified to assess confidence in answering questions once the vaccine becomes available. For survey respondents with lower literacy levels, a visual response scale can be used. This scale is designed for questions with four response options, such as Not at all, A little, Moderately, and Very. In contexts where multiple COVID-19 vaccines are available, questions should be modified to refer to the COVID-19 vaccines collectively. It may also be useful to explore whether perceptions, norms, and willingness to accept a vaccine depend on the specific vaccine being offered. Interviewers should probe for opinions on all vaccines available in the local context. If vaccines are not yet available, the questions should be adjusted accordingly. Health workers may also be asked about their perceived risk of contracting COVID-19, their concerns about transmitting the virus to patients, and their experiences with stigma related to being a healthcare worker during the pandemic. For example, they might be asked, How concerned are you about getting COVID-19? or What do you think about the risk of transmitting COVID-19 to your patients? These questions aim to understand their perceived risks and experiences. Questions about COVID-19 vaccine confidence could include, How do you feel about the COVID-19 vaccine(s)? Probes might explore perceptions of safety, efficacy, and alignment with personal or religious beliefs. If multiple vaccines are available, perceptions of each should be assessed. Additionally, participants could be asked about their thoughts on the safety of the vaccine, concerns about its novelty, and whether they believe it works. To understand practical issues, participants might be asked about their experiences with previous vaccinations, such as, Have you ever had a vaccine as an adult? What do you remember about it? Probes could explore both positive and negative experiences, as well as logistical challenges like cost, transportation, or time off work. Finally, cognitive interviewing is recommended to improve the quality of survey questions and response options. Feedback from these interviews can be used to refine the survey before broader implementation.
